question: What reforms, if any, are being implemented at present?
item: Key Public Financial Management (PFM) processes (please type your responses and, if possible, provide examples include a description of the following: 1) Implementation status 2) Timelines 3) Milestones achieved 4) Milestones to achieve 5) Responsible agency for implementation 6) Donor partners, keeping each response below 2,000 characters (as counted below the text box))
answer:
Current PFM reforms in Côte d’Ivoire focus on continued implementation of the Schéma Directeur de la Réforme des Finances Publiques (public finance reform master plan). According to the 2025-2027 DPBEP annex, implementation is ongoing. Key milestones already achieved include production of annual performance reports and the general performance report, production of program performance audit reports, organization of the Budget Orientation Debate, and strengthened assessment/publication of the “Déclaration sur les Risques Budgétaires.” Another ongoing reform is extension of SIGOBE to national public establishments and all national representations abroad.

In budget and expenditure management, earlier DPBEP documentation also highlights the transition to programme-based budgeting, deployment of SIGFIP in embassies and interior localities, reinforcement of internal control arrangements, and wider dissemination of fiscal information through the citizen’s budget. These indicate a medium-term reform path already underway, with further milestones centered on broader system rollout, stronger performance management, and improved fiscal risk oversight.

In public procurement, reforms under implementation include continued dematerialization/digitalization of procurement procedures, reduction of exceptional/derogatory procedures in favor of competitive methods, gradual connection of public establishments, local governments, and state-owned enterprises to SIGOMAP/SIGMAP, continued efforts to shorten procurement timelines, online accessibility of SIGMAP, and continuous updating of the reference price database. Achieved milestones include the launch and progressive deployment of SIGMAP/SIGOMAP and maintenance of the price reference database since 2020; remaining milestones appear to involve completing broader connection of covered entities and further reducing delays.

The responsible implementing agencies are not fully specified in the excerpts, but they appear to sit mainly within the Ministry of Finance/Budget architecture, especially the DGBF and institutions managing public procurement systems. No donor partners are identified in the retrieved text.

question: Please identify the key laws and regulations that govern PFM in your country, clarifying which legal provisions have higher authority and which are lower-tier regulations following the hierarchy of the legislative framework. Extract up to 10 laws, ordered from highest authority to lowest.
answer:
Estonia’s PFM framework can be ordered by legal authority as follows. Instruments within the same tier are not ranked against one another:

1. Constitution of the Republic of Estonia (Eesti Vabariigi põhiseadus) — the highest domestic legal authority.
2. State Budget Act (Riigieelarve seadus) — a parliamentary Act governing the state budget. The Ministry of Finance expressly cites § 75 as a basis for its budget-execution overview.
3. Accounting Act (Raamatupidamise seadus) — a parliamentary Act establishing the accounting framework.
4. Local Government Financial Management Act (Kohaliku omavalitsuse üksuse finantsjuhtimise seadus, KOFS) — a parliamentary Act concerning local-government finances, rather than central-government budgeting.
5. Structural Support Act (Struktuuritoetuste seadus) — identified in the drafts as primary legislation concerning structural-support funds; the cited passage does not establish which version is currently applicable.
6. Government of the Republic Regulation No. 112 of 19 December 2019 — a subordinate regulation covering preparation of the state budget strategy and draft budget, transfers of budget funds, and reporting under the State Budget Act. The Ministry expressly cites § 17 alongside State Budget Act § 75.
7. Regulation on preparing, implementing, reporting on, evaluating and amending sectoral development plans and programmes — identified as a lower-tier planning regulation; its current status is not established by the cited passage.
8. Procedure for allocating funds from the Government reserve and using allocated funds — a lower-tier reserve-fund procedure identified in the drafts.
9. Budget Classification (Eelarveklassifikaator) — a lower-tier budget-classification instrument identified in the drafts.
10. Public-Sector Financial Accounting and Reporting Guideline (Avaliku sektori finantsarvestuse ja -aruandluse juhend) — lower-tier accounting and reporting guidance identified in the drafts.

The hierarchy is constitutional provisions above parliamentary Acts, with implementing regulations and administrative instruments below Acts. Only the State Budget Act and Regulation No. 112 are directly substantiated by the quoted Ministry passage; the descriptions and current applicability of the other instruments are not independently established by that passage.

question: Please identify the key laws and regulations that govern PFM in your country, clarifying which legal provisions have higher authority and which are lower-tier regulations following the hierarchy of the legislative framework. Extract up to 10 laws, ordered from highest authority to lowest.
answer:
Ghana’s PFM legal framework, ordered from higher to lower legal authority, is:

1. Constitution of the Republic of Ghana, 1992 — constitutional tier.
2. Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921) — Act of Parliament.
3. Public Procurement Act, 2003 (Act 663), as amended — Act of Parliament.
4. Internal Audit Agency Act, 2003 (Act 658) — Act of Parliament.
5. Public Financial Management Regulations, 2019 (L.I. 2378) — implementing regulations under the PFM Act.

Acts of Parliament are at the statutory tier below the Constitution. Legislative Instruments and other regulations are lower-tier instruments implementing statutory provisions. Ministerial guidelines, such as the PFM Commitment Control Guidelines, are administrative guidance rather than laws or regulations; the Ministry states that applicable PFM laws prevail where a guideline conflicts with them.

question: What reforms, if any, are being implemented at present?
item: Key Public Financial Management (PFM) processes (please type your responses and, if possible, provide examples include a description of the following: 1) Implementation status 2) Timelines 3) Milestones achieved 4) Milestones to achieve 5) Responsible agency for implementation 6) Donor partners, keeping each response below 2,000 characters (as counted below the text box))
answer:
Kenya is currently implementing its third Public Financial Management (PFM) Reform Strategy covering 2018-2023, guided by Medium-Term Plan III. According to the PEFA 2022 report, reform implementation was ongoing at the time of reporting, and about 60% of planned reforms had either been achieved or were at various stages of completion. Progress was negatively affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, although funding remained available.

Implementation status and scope: The ongoing reform agenda is organized around eight result areas: (1) sustainable and predictable fiscal space to deliver government programs; (2) strategic and transparent spending on public investment and service delivery in line with national and county policy commitments; (3) reliable cash for service delivery and public investment; (4) value for money in procurement and contract management; (5) value for money, performance and accountability in staffing for service delivery; (6) education institutions, health facilities and other service delivery units effectively managing public resources; (7) disciplined financial management and accurate reporting; and (8) accountability through audit, oversight and follow-up.

Timelines: The current formal reform window is 2018-2023. Earlier reform phases included the 2006-2011 strategy and the 2013-2018 PFM reform strategy.

Milestones achieved/examples: Reported achievements across reform periods include progress in IFMIS reengineering, strengthening of expenditure controls, improvements in revenue administration, budget execution, accounting and reporting, and stronger internal controls covering payroll, procurement, non-salary expenditure and internal audit. The 2013-2018 reform documents also cite establishment of the Public Sector Accounting Standards Board (PSASB), adoption/pronouncement of public sector accounting standards, preparation of consolidated financial statements for FY 2013/14 and FY 2014/15 within statutory timelines, and gazetting of the PFM Regulations 2015.

Milestones to achieve: The remaining agenda is to complete unfinished reforms under the eight result areas, especially those delayed by capacity constraints, sequencing issues, and COVID-19 disruptions.

Responsible agency: The Government of Kenya is responsible overall, with implementation anchored in the national PFM reform framework and Ministry of Finance/National Treasury-led processes; specific actions also involve sector institutions and oversight/accountability bodies.

Donor partners: The provided excerpts refer to partnerships with development partners within a coordinated framework, but do not identify specific donor partners by name.

Nigeria’s federal PFM framework can be arranged by legal tier as follows. The order within the Acts tier is illustrative: the retrieved evidence does not establish that one listed Act has higher authority than another.

1. Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended) — highest authority and the constitutional framework for public finance.
2. Finance (Control and Management) Act, 1958 (cited in the Financial Regulations as Cap. 144, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 1990) — primary legislation for federal financial control and accounting.
3. Annual and supplementary Appropriation Acts — primary legislation authorising the expenditure to which they relate; the retrieved excerpts identify these categories but give no particular Act or year.
4. Fiscal Responsibility Act, 2007 — primary legislation in the fiscal-responsibility framework.
5. Public Procurement Act, 2007 — primary legislation governing public procurement.
6. Financial Reporting Council Act, 2011 — primary legislation relevant to financial reporting and accountability.
7. Pension Reform Act, 2014 (as amended) — primary legislation relevant to pension finances.
8. Finance Act, 2022 — primary legislation identified in the evidence as supporting fiscal-consolidation measures.
9. Federal Government Financial Regulations (revised October 2009) — lower-tier rules for federal financial administration, beneath the Constitution and Acts.
10. Treasury Circulars — administrative instructions below Acts and Financial Regulations (inferred hierarchical placement). A cited 2024 Public Finance Management Bill discusses their application, but its enactment is not established; that Bill is therefore not listed as a law in force.

The Auditor-General’s report also identifies the Companies and Allied Matters Act among legislation relevant to the PFM framework. Its inclusion does not establish a separate rank among the Acts above.

Timelines: Main reform period is 2024–2028. Some reforms build on earlier initiatives that remain ongoing, including UACS, TSA, electronic payments, cash budgeting, and internal audit improvements.

Milestones achieved: Prior roadmaps and ongoing reforms have already delivered important milestones, including program expenditure classification and performance-informed budgeting, implementation of the Treasury Single Account, establishment of the Unified Accounts Code Structure (UACS), automation of various PFM functions, introduction of citizen and performance audits, establishment of a PFM competency framework, and conduct of capacity-building programs.

answer:
The Philippines is implementing ongoing reforms to strengthen and fully institutionalize its Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS). Implementation is already underway rather than at a purely design stage: the government has rolled out key building blocks since 2010, and Executive Order No. 29, s. 2023 directed the full adoption/implementation of IFMIS across government agencies. Under the Public Financial Management Reforms Roadmap 2024–2028, the main strategy is to develop and implement the Budget and Treasury Management System (BTMS) as the interoperable core of IFMIS, while linking existing stand-alone and legacy systems through APIs to reduce disruption.

Timelines: foundational reforms began in 2010; several roadmap reforms remained ongoing after 2016; the MOA on Budget Reforms in 2018 accelerated digital budgeting tools; EO No. 29 in 2023 renewed the mandate for full implementation; and the current reform roadmap covers 2024–2028.

Milestones achieved: rollout of key PFM digital components including the Unified Accounts Code Structure (UACS), Treasury Single Account (TSA), Online Submission of Budget Proposals System (OSBPS), Unified Reporting System (URS), and adoption of BTMS-related digital reforms. The government has also harmonized account codes and improved online, real-time budget and cash management processes.

Milestones to achieve: full government-wide IFMIS adoption; further BTMS development and quality controls; integration/harmonization of agency systems; establishment of PFM data management architecture and a comprehensive data lake/warehouse; and continued institutionalization through legislation such as the Progressive Budgeting for Better and Modernized Governance Bill.

Responsible agencies: Department of Budget and Management (DBM), Department of Finance (DOF), and Bureau of the Treasury (BTr), with Commission on Audit (COA) involved in the broader PFM framework.

question: Please identify the key laws and regulations that govern PFM in your country, clarifying which legal provisions have higher authority and which are lower-tier regulations following the hierarchy of the legislative framework. Extract up to 10 laws, ordered from highest authority to lowest.
answer:
The key laws and regulations governing PFM in Uzbekistan, ordered from highest to lowest authority, are:

1. Constitution of the Republic of Uzbekistan – Highest legal authority, referenced in the Budget Code and foundational for all legislation.
2. Budget Code of the Republic of Uzbekistan – Organic budget law adopted in 2013, primary framework for the budget system and process.
3. Annual Law on the State Budget – Enacted each year by Parliament, sets appropriations and fiscal rules for the year.
4. Presidential Decrees – Issued to supplement budget laws and adjust fiscal parameters; have force of law.
5. Resolutions of the Cabinet of Ministers – Secondary legislation implementing Budget Code provisions and budget execution.
6. Orders and Normative Acts of the Ministry of Economy and Finance – Include technical instructions, budget classification, and treasury regulations.
7. Instructions on Budget Classification – Lower-tier regulation specifying application of budget classification.
8. Treasury Circulars and Budget Circulars – Operational guidance for budget preparation and execution.
9. International Treaties – Supersede national law where applicable, as per the Budget System Law.
10. Earlier Law on the Budget System – Predecessor to the Budget Code, referenced for continuity provisions but largely superseded.

This hierarchy is directly evidenced in Uzbekistan's official legal database and the Budget Code, with additional detail from PEFA and official government sources. The Tax Code and Central Bank regulations, while relevant to fiscal management, are not directly evidenced as core PFM laws in the retrieved material and are therefore omitted.

18. The government has taken actions to improve debt and fiscal risk management. The May 2023 public debt law requires the government to prepare a public debt management strategy and an annual borrowing plan and includes several provisions that facilitate fiscal risk management. It sets a debt ceiling of 60 percent of GDP on PPG debt and requires government action to prevent a breach if PPG debt reaches 50 percent of GDP. The law also establishes conditions for providing state guarantees and gives authority to the government to set ceilings on guarantees, including a separate one for PPP-related guarantees. PPPs have grown rapidly in recent years, amounting to a cumulative 20 percent of GDP at end-2023.

The authorities have made notable progress towards addressing some public financial management (PFM) challenges experienced in recent years, in line with IMF CD advice. Uzbekistan's Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) reforms are a core component of the 2020–2024 Public Financial Management (PFM) Strategy. The system comprises the Government Financial Management Information System (GFMIS) for budget execution and UzASBO 2.0 for budget preparation and execution. 

1) Implementation status: IT systems have been expanded to underpin PFM outcomes, with GFMIS and UzASBO 2.0 both operational. Integration between the two platforms is ongoing and remains a priority. 2) Timelines: The reforms are guided by the 2020–2024 PFM Strategy, though implementation has faced some delays and gaps.

3) Milestones achieved: GFMIS is operational for budget execution; UzASBO 2.0 is deployed for budget preparation and execution; commitment control is effective and has limited arrears; real-time/near-real-time financial data is available.

4) Milestones to achieve: Full integration of GFMIS and UzASBO 2.0; enhanced IT support for annual and medium-term budget submissions by line agencies and territorial entities; improved public availability of investment, fiscal risk, and debt strategy information.

5) Responsible agency: The Ministry of Economy and Finance (MOEF), reorganized from the Ministry of Finance as of January 1, 2023, leads implementation.

6) Donor partners: While not explicitly named for IFMIS in the cited evidence, the World Bank and IMF are active in Uzbekistan's broader PFM reform program.

answer:
Uzbekistan is actively implementing institutional capacity building reforms as part of its broader 2020–2025 Public Financial Management (PFM) reform program. 

1) Implementation status: Ongoing. The Ministry of Finance is leading government-wide PFM reforms, including the rollout of an Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS), strengthening internal and external audit functions, improving fiscal discipline, and enhancing macro-fiscal planning and forecasting. The Central Bank and the Agency of Guarantee Citizens' Deposits in Banks are also undertaking sector-specific capacity reforms, such as the establishment of a Research Council, adoption of the Paybox Plus model, and development of a Management Information System.

2) Timelines: The main PFM reform program spans 2020–2025. Central Bank and deposit guarantee agency reforms are active in 2025 and 2026.

3) Milestones achieved: Mature audit processes are in place; a Chart of Accounts enabling multi-dimensional expenditure analysis has been implemented; IFMIS is operational; strong treasury operations and cash management are functioning; a Roadmap based on World Bank recommendations is underway; a three-year audit cycle aligned with Global Internal Audit Standards has been introduced; technical assistance missions from the IMF have been conducted.

4) Milestones to achieve: Full rollout of medium-term expenditure budgeting and linkage to strategic plans; improvement of non-financial performance and outcome indicators; further harmonization with international standards; completion of program budget approach integration; expanded IFMIS coverage.

5) Responsible agencies: Ministry of Finance (PFM reforms), Central Bank of Uzbekistan (financial sector capacity), Agency of Guarantee Citizens' Deposits in Banks (deposit guarantee reform).

6) Donor partners: World Bank (PFM and deposit guarantee agency), IMF (technical assistance), KOICA (grant funding for Management Information System), European Union (PFM support).
